review:
Let's get this out of the way, I'm a big fan of vampire RPGs. I consider the OG Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines to be one of the greatest RPGs ever made, so I'm always busy looking for something that can scratch that particular itch. The Blood of Dawnwalker definitely did that for me and I in return fully sunk my teeth into it!

This game is pretty much everything I wanted it to be. It's not perfect by all means, but the atmosphere, the world, the characters and especially the freedom you have in shaping your own adventure are fantastic.

One of the things I enjoyed the most is how organically you can find and start quests. You can simply stumble across something happening in the world, find a quest item on an enemy you just fought, or simply come across something while exploring that pulls you into a completely unexpected situation. There's something really satisfying about not having every single quest handed to you by an NPC with a marker above their head. It makes exploring feel worthwhile, and it's one of my favorite things about RPGs in general.

The time system is another thing I really liked. Having that clock constantly ticking in the background makes even small decisions feel like they could have consequences later. You can't do everything, and I actually think that's a good thing. Sometimes you have to choose what matters to you and accept that something else might happen without you. It makes the world feel like it's actually moving rather than waiting for the player.

My only real issue with the time system is that learning skills and perks also takes up time. I don't mind quests taking up time at all, that's part of what makes the system interesting. But losing a time slot just because you wanted to learn something new feels a bit like being punished for engaging with the progression system. I'd rather spend that time actually doing something in the world.

The combat takes a little getting used to, but it mostly clicks by the end of the prologue. Once you have more abilities and start figuring out how everything works together, you can pull off some pretty fun stuff. It's not the main reason I'm playing Dawnwalker, but it gets the job done.

What really makes the game work for me is how ambitious it is. It feels like the developers genuinely wanted to give the player room to make their own story instead of creating a world where there is always one obvious "correct" way to do things. Your choices matter, sometimes in ways you don't immediately realize, and I really like that approach.

I'm also really happy to see Rebel Wolves doing well with the game. A new studio taking on an RPG this ambitious is a pretty big gamble, so seeing the game succeed makes me even more excited for what's next.

If this really is the beginning of the larger saga they've talked about, I'm absolutely here for it. The idea of seeing this world evolve, especially with the hints we've already gotten about future time periods, is something I'm genuinely looking forward to.

I'm far from being done with the game, but I just find myself completely lost in it every time I click the "Play" button and I think this is one of the biggest compliments I can give to Rebel Wolves, so I wanted to share my thoughts asap!

As a massive The Witcher fan, my hype levels were through the roof when I found out this game was made by the Witcher devs. You can practically smell the dark, gritty fantasy DNA the second you enter the game. The atmosphere is top-tier, but after putting some real time into it, I need to be honest: it is not a perfect game.

First, the good stuff: I really like the combat. It feels sharp and weighty, and pairing traditional swordplay with supernatural abilities gives a genuinely satisfying rhythm to every encounter.

The biggest surprise for me was the pacing. I have never played a game with a time limit before, and usually, that kind of pressure stresses me out. But against all odds, I actually like the mechanic here. It forces you to make meaningful, tense choices about how you spend your days, adding a layer of strategy I didn't expect to enjoy.

The story so far is great. I can count on the fingers of one hand the amount of good vampire story games I've played, and this is by far one of the best.

Now for the bad: the performance absolutely needs to be fixed. The frame rate dips heavily in dense areas, and the optimization is rough around the edges. I absolutely hate that I need to press a key to switch between abilities and potions. I'm playing on PC put a damn hotbar from 1 through 9 for the items I could use!

My Verdict: Although it is a great game at its core with an awesome world, the technical hiccups and minor bugs drag it down. Some animations need to be polished, as they sometimes feel robotic, and the lipsyncing is a little bit off, which leads to a few NPCs not moving their mouths at all. I would highly recommend buying it if you love narrative-driven RPGs, because its strongest point is there. If you are a The Witcher 3 fan, you will absolutely love this game because it takes a lot from it. After a few patches that fix the performance, bugs and some animations, I'm sure that this game is going to be a gem.

I admit it: At first, this game really did not appeal to me. 

This game was directed by the director of Witcher 3, and features a lot of the staff of that game. Now, I'm a massive fan of Witcher 3 - It's one of my absolute favorite games of all-time. But I am just not super into vampire fiction. A game that revolves around it is really just not for me.

Or so I thought. 

The Blood of Dawnwalker absolutely wears its inspirations on its sleeve. Two parts Witcher 3, one part Vampire The Masquerade Bloodlines, one-half part Kingdom Come Deliverance. And it all works really, really well. 

I read some criticism of the writing, but I really cannot get behind that whatsoever. The writing is really sharp. Dialogue is good, characters are excellent. There's a nice narrative hook in the main story, and the power fantasy is certainly here as well. Riding along with Coen going from a stressed out youth caring for his sick mother and young siblings to an all-powerful Vampire that's feared by the entire Vale of Sangora is quite the ride. 

Most noteworthy is the high level of effort put into a lot of the side content. You can see the Witcher 3 experience there; the side quests are populated with interesting characters, and there is far more branching quest design here than ever there was in Witcher 3, which was pretty straightforward by comparison. 

Quests in Dawnwalker change drastically depending on your choice. I've replayed several of them and been quite surprised by what I thought to be a relatively minor decision turning into a major change for the side quest in question. And they all make sense: Those twists based on your decisions never feel arbitrary. They always result in a, "Oh shoot, I should've considered that" kind of thought. That's something that must incredibly hard for the devs to design for, but they nailed it here. 

Most surprising for me was the combat. I expected it to be rough and janky; something like Witcher 2, but it's not. It's surprisingly snappy, quick, and addictive. I applaud the devs for not going the easy "let's just rip off Dark Souls" route, and instead taking their inspiration straight from Kingdom Come Deliverance's directional parries and attacks system (which I adored!). This is a game in which I'll beat my head against the wall for hours, fighting an enemy I absolutely should not be fighting because I'm way underleveled, but repeatedly trying it anyway because the combat is so weighty, impactful, and satisfying. 

There are some "go here and kill all the bad guys" side content, but it never quite becomes dull because the combat is so entertaining. It never gets old ripping apart human enemies at night as a vampire. 

I will levy one criticism at the character movement: Coen moves so tanky and takes time to turn, which, humorously enough, is a criticism I had of Witcher 3 as well! The DNA shows there. It's very irritating trying to maneuver Coen through tighter spaces like inside homes, and I recall having that very same issue with Witcher 3. 

Character-building is also really fun. You have three basic trees: Swordplay, Witchcraft, and Vampirism. Each have their own impacts, upgrades for each are floored in entirely different aspects (you need skill books to improve swordplay, you need to increase your corruption by feeding on the blood of humans and animals for vampirism, etc.) and they're all hyper-addictive to engage with as you roam around the map and complete various well-written side content. 

The main quest timer has been controversial, but I'm glad the developers tried something bold and new. I actually really like the notion for an open world game; I'm a completely addicted completionist. I cannot stop myself from clearing every map marker, and that sometimes bogs me down in open world games (looking at you, Assassin's Creed). I like that the timer in Dawnwalker forces me to prioritize and choose! The main quest timer gives you plenty of slack to get the important things done, so it's not a huge constraint unless you're really being careless with how you're spending your time. 

Further, I think it should be made clear that this isn't a ticking clock. It's a set of 8 blocks you spend (different quests cost different blocks, with most only costing you a single block of time), which is good. I tend to play games very slowly; I like to investigate everything, wander around, take in the views, etc. A ticking clock would've killed the experience for me. The timer in this game is more of a resource to be spent strategically, and I think that really works for this game. If you're worried about that and avoiding this game as a result: Don't be. You're missing out on a really enjoyable game. 

The one area I will criticize is the feature in which upgrading most of your skills costs a block of time. This is, frankly, stupid. There's no real logical reason it should do so, and it really only serves to stifle exploration into different skills. I'm spending most of my time traversing around with a million unused skill points and using them when I find something that requires them, which is not the experience I think the devs want. Skill points should be driving the dopamine drip, and they don't here because of the way the game ties them into the timer system. 

That said, the rest of this game's foundation is good enough to keep you driving along. The story is really good, the main character is likable, it's fun to engage with. The worldbuilding is also superb - Great job to the writing team there as building an entire world in lockstep with a brand new video game cannot be easy. Additionally, the music is excellent! 

If you liked Witcher 3, Kingdom Come Deliverance's combat, open world games or cinematic RPGs like Mass Effect, or are a fanatic for vampire fiction, I honestly think one's worth it at full price. I expected a janky, rough-around-the-edges AA game, but it's got a lot more heart and polish than that, particularly in its writing, world, and combat. 

Thanks and congratulations, Rebel Wolves. You guys nailed it. Can't wait to see what you do next in this world.

Honestly, I stumbled upon a game that turned out way better than I expected. After all the recent disappointments, playing a proper vampire game felt exceptionally goood. We're in the mid ages, and humanity is literally gasping for breath due to the plague; the vampire race (Vrakhir), ruled by a bald lunatic psycho named Brencis, offers their own blood as a cure for this disease, but in doing so, they end up enslaving humans. In the midst of all this, we go through some personal drama while trying to save our lovely family from Brencis's clutches.

Our main character, Coen, is a total wildcard.. depending on your choices, he becomes either an absolute maniac or a complete paragon of virtue. Depending on which direction you develop your skills, your notoriety increases, and killing people directly affects your reputation and even your savagery.

I found the main storyline quite engaging. Without giving away any spoilers, I can say this: the replayability of this game is extremely high. I was most surprise by how a simple side quest you start purely out of curiosity ends up impacting the main story to such a massive degree.

I'd suggest paying close attention to time in the game because time is a critical factor yayy! You need to get certain things done within a given time frame or things quickly go sideways.. Time even passes while you r upgrading skills, so you really have to plan meticulously. The day night cycle adds a completely different atmosphere to the game. We are a "Dawnwalker," a different type of Vrakhir to put it simply, during the day you're a young, black haired Geralt, and at night you r a vampire, black haired Geralt. And yes, we are much, much stronger at night...

Yea, soundtrack isnt bad, but don't expect bangers on the level of Witcher 2 or 3. That said, I can comfortably say the combat mechanics are better than Witcher 3 they feel much more fluid and responsive. Aaa there's a woman named Xanthe, and shes the one I'm most terified of I was just thinking, "I hope she pops up near the end of the game so I can take her down with my newly unlocked high/usefull skills." Right before writing this review, I ran into her, and let's just say our meeting didn't go so welll. Long story short, I dont get along well with women in real life, and nothing changed here either... 

The map feels both huge and packed with content. I dont know, maybe it feels that way because I haven't played a decent game in a long time, but Blood of dawnwalker managed to leave me really satisfied on the content front. As for optimization, it is typical Unreal engine 5 stuff.. Don't go in with massive expectations, but it's not bad. On my weary RTX 4070 that keeps trying its best, I haven't had any major issues yet with Dlss and Frame generation enabled.

Overall, I'm really pleased with Blood of Dawnwalker. I didnt want to write a review right away because I expected it to start strong and then become generic, but I'm glad I waited. It turned out muuch better than I thought. The Rebel Wolves team did a great job, hats off to them!

This is Vampire done right. None of that Twilight bull****. This is Nosferatu reinvented.

I am not going to lie, at first I was a bit disappointed. I went into this thinking it was something else. I looked at the tags and saw "action adventure" and was expecting more of that. This is VERY MUCH more of an action RPG game, leaning heavily into the narrative elements to start. Think 'The Witcher' meets 'KCD2'. 

That being said, you need to give this game time to see the true [i]action[/i] part. It very slowly sets the stage and tone. The prologue can easily take 2-4 hours to complete if you are like me and need to a) loot/steal everything, b) try to complete every quest and c) explore every nook and cranny/unlock all the fast travel hearths. If that sounds like you, be prepared for very light combat (barely scratches the surface of what you can do) and more back and forth questing that can seem rather dull, but it is more to ease you into all the basic mechanics. Once you get past the prologue, the whole world map opens up. And this is where the real fun begins. 

I can't believe I am saying this (because I hate soul like games and block/parry based mechanics) but the coordinated blocking in this game is my favourite part. It feels so satisfying. Instead of just pressing the block button to block, you also need to press a directional button to block incoming attacks (for example: left block, right block, up block, down block). Sounds like a lot but the tutorials are great and there are different difficulty modes and prompts that can be enabled to let you know what direction you need to block in, with options for an auto block in the settings (still need to press block but you won't be penalized with health if you press the wrong directional key, it just uses up stamina). The directional key thing is also applicable for combat which I found pretty unique. 

I don't want to give away the story or spoil the discovery at all, but in addition to swordplay there are multiple skill trees dabbling in both vampirism and witchcraft that you allocate points into. The combat really evolves over time and I love how you actually feel like you are a vampire with the abilities you can use, in and out of combat. You can bite to recover health, crawl up walls, teleport. My only complaint with combat are the controls. You cannot remap keys. And I find it a bit cumbersome to navigate through the inventory and ability wheels during combat. Just a lot of unnecessary button pressing. Ain't no one got time for all that mid combat -_- 

Once the whole map opens up, it very much is open world with guided questing and a progressing storyline. But there are limitations to be aware of. You only have a set amount of time during the day and night. Completing missions and tasks, eats up time. You also have a set amount of days to complete the main storyline. So you need to be aware of that and sometimes, choose your activities wisely. Some are time sensitive. Decisions appear to shape and matter in this game. They did a really good job with the RPG elements and allowing you to play the way you want to play. Only complaint being… how you gonna have an open world and no mini map?? 

If you are having a hard time getting through the prologue, push past that. It is but a sliver of the gameplay. You will be rewarded with not only beautiful graphics, great characters and an engaging story but vampire lore that is effortlessly weaved into every aspect of the game. 

It is not everyday vampire fans get something like this, so enjoy!!

[b]Update:[/b]
For people worried about time management…
[spoiler] The main storyline quests will tell you if you are high enough level to progress (it says stuff like ‘at your current level this will be a challenge’ in orange text). So what I am doing is using this as an indicator when I need to do some quests on the side to level up vs if I should be progressing the story along. Hopefully it doesn’t screw me over but I’m assuming that is why they incorporated comments like that. Good luck!! [/spoiler]

As a huge fan of vampires and all the folklore surrounding them, its really not easy when it comes to games.

For one thing, games set in a vampire universe are very rare, and the ones that do exist are mostly either watered down with the worst clichés or just pure junk from top to bottom.
In my opinion, the only really good games set in the vampire universe are the Legacy of Kain series and Vampire: The Masquerade. There are other “okayish” vampire games, but personally I wouldnt consider BloodRayne a top tier title, for example.
And now comes The Blood of Dawnwalker!
Basically, for me its The Witcher 3 in vampire clothing. Thankfully with a fun combat system. I found the combat in The Witcher absolutely dreadful and completely devoid of fun.

The combat system in Dawnwalker isnt extremely complex, but its just fun and works flawlessly. Its similar to the one in Kingdom Come: Deliverance, where you can attack and parry from four different directions. Its incredibly satisfying when you knock an opponent off their feet and they are hurled through the air, gurgling.
I could go into detail about the individual skill trees, but that would go beyond the scope of this post. Just briefly: I actually found that every skill serves a purpose, and none of them seemed useless to me. My favorite skill is the one where you simply make the enemy explode.
The entire world is incredibly beautiful, gloomy, filthy, and merciless. In Dawnwalker theres no joy, everything is simply terrible, and everyone suffers. Just as it should be in dark fantasy!

Theres something to discover everywhere. The world is inhabited by all sorts of creatures, such as goat people, fat elves, ghouls, and much more.
The characters are all well developed too, and I didnt come across a single one where I thought, “Well, that one isnt so great.” They are all very different characters, all trying to ease their suffering their own way.
Coen is also an extremely good main character whom I enjoyed playing, because hes very likable right from the start.

The quest design is also extremely good. No quest is boring. There are no cheap fetch quests like in other games where you just mindlessly run around the area doing things like “collect 100 of this or that” or “talk to person A and then talk to person B.”

Every quest has its own story. Sometimes its a short little story, but most of the time its quest chains with fairly long and detailed stories. In any case, I wasnt bored at any point, and I didnt find a single quest to be bad. There is a bit of collecting stuff, but thats really limited to checking off fast travel points or clearing small camps of jerks.
In any case, its not overloaded, and definitely not Ubisoft-style “I cant see the map because its covered in icons.”

Just a quick note about the time limit that many people criticized beforehand: I dont think anyone likes time limits. I, for one, hate them. But I can say that in Dawnwalker, its absolutely no problem. It doesnt stress you out at all, and you dont feel any pressure or anything like that. I was able to do everything I wanted to do, and I still had 5 days left at the end. The time limit is just part of the narrative, but it doesnt really affect the gameplay itself.

My only real criticism of the game is the traversal at times. When you try to climb a wall or run over some boulders, it can feel pretty clunky. It wasnt a dealbreaker for me, but it definitely needs a bit more polish.

For me, The Blood of Dawnwalker is a strong contender for GOTY 2026, and the game truly deserves to be played.
If you liked The Witcher 3, then you will like Dawnwalker too. And if you like vampire games on top, then this is your wildest dream come true!
Ignore haters. This game is absoloutly fantastic. Finally a game with some balls to try something new. We should encourage this

In terms of how your decisions matter, Dawnwalker teaches you early on that there isn't the "right" solution (just how it was in Witcher and BG3) and that [b]every coin has two sides to it[/b]. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a breath of fresh air for the action-RPG genre. For the first time in a long time, it gives RPG players agency over the narrative and 'choice and consequence' are more than just simple buzz words used to market the game. 

There are many fantastic, AA or AAA RPGs over recent years, but nearly all of them fail to deliver on the 'choice and consequence' expectations that many RPG players expect. Recent Bethesda titles, such as Skyrim or Starfield, offer a sandbox experience, but allow players to do everything and experience everything in one playthrough, with side quests and the ‘main quest’ nicely sliced and treated separately from each other. As a way to illustrate this point: so you’re on the big quest to stop big bad evil, great, but you’ve also taken a significant amount of time to join the thieves’ guild while the world stops and waits for you to pick up on the main quest again. This probably works well for casual players, but not for die-hard RPG fans looking for something different. Even more recent immersive RPGs, such as KCD II or the Gothic 1 remake, while offering a more narrative-focused experience, still force the player to follow a linear series of quests until they reach the end of the game with little to no agency over how the narrative plays out. In such games, where the player can make a choice, it is actually not telegraphed whilst the player is playing the game, but rather is displayed as part of an ending cinematic or narrated after you put down the controller or step away from the keyboard. A similar game, not in terms of gameplay or overall narrative, but in terms of experimental structure and quest design that resonated with me whilst playing this game, was Dontnod's 2018 'Vampyr'. If you enjoyed what Vampyr tried to do with its progression and quest design, but forgave some of its less polished faults, you will also enjoy Blood of Dawnwalker.

In Blood of Dawnwalker, by having one main goal (with no linear progression) supported by a series of optional quests, which can have a variety of outcomes, depending on when the player decides to start the quest or what time of day they complete it, really adds weight to the choices that the player has to make. This is further supported by treating time as a resource, where undertaking certain quests or actions can eat into the 30 days that you have to complete the main goal of the game. It’s not for everyone and will anger completionist players who like to do everything in one playthrough, but it is different and is probably one of the best innovations to the RPG genre in recent years.
All of this is supported by an extremely dark atmosphere, both in terms of the visual presentation of the game and the narrative, which sets it apart from similar titles that tackle the same subject matter, such Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines 2. Everything from the voice acting to the quest design is executed well; it doesn’t work all the time, but when it does it can really pull you in. Whether it’s saving a rebel working against the vampire overlords or helping a vampire who uses his faith in Christianity to stop himself from feeding on human blood; nothing is clearly black and white, or can be placed in ‘good’ and ‘evil’ camps, and you will always be surprised by what you might receive at the end of the quest – perhaps it’s a powerful object or an alliance with the quest giver. Do you lead more in to Coen’s vampiric side, spending most of your time levelling up his vampiric powers and undertaking quests at night, perhaps siding with some other potential vampire allies, or do you perhaps want to roleplay Coen as a bastion of humanity, doing everything you can do avoid having to play as a vampire, skipping night time and investing in your human abilities, siding with human characters (some good, some more morally complex); or perhaps you want to roleplay as the titular Dawnwalker, taking advantage of both day and night and building a jack-of-all trades build and building a coalition of forces to take down Brencis and his vampire allies. The game lets you play out these fantasies and does not punish you for choosing a particular way to play the game.

If you like dark, western action-RPGs, with gameplay similar to the Witcher and want to experience a new experimental method to narrative and storytelling, then you must play this game.

I honestly started this game quite blind. I wishlisted it when it was announced but didn’t pay much attention, the “new IP from former big-studio veterans” trope often ends up mediocre (looking at you, Back 4 Blood). I waited for release and the first reviews. 

Overall this is a solid AA game. Almost every system has something good or even great, but you can clearly see the AA limitations. It’s not perfect and has its issues, yet it’s never bad. As a package it works. You can feel the former CDPR veterans’ experience from the start (I had just begun replaying The Witcher 3), but where that game feels polished and streamlined, Dawnwalker is more uneven. Its peaks are excellent, the flaws easier to spot. It’s like a pretty lake on a hot day: inviting and refreshing, but a bit shallow.

The most polarizing mechanic is time. Every day is split into day and night, each with 8 time units. Meaningful actions, quests, some activities, even leveling, advance the clock. After the prologue you get 30 days and nights for the main goal. Missing the deadline isn’t a game over, but the pressure is real. This creates a lot of friction, especially for completionists. You either adapt or decide it’s not for you. It isn’t perfect. Spending time on skill unlocks and empty chests feels particularly lame. The early hours can feel overwhelming, but eventually you learn to manage your time and accept you can’t do everything. There’s still plenty to experience in one playthrough. 
Exploration thankfully doesn’t cost time, the world is huge, handcrafted, and worth wandering, though running around early on gets tiring without movement skills. The game is clearly built for multiple playthroughs (New Game+ is planned but by the time I wrote this review isn't implemented yet).

You play as Coen, a peasant who becomes a Dawnwalker, human by day, vampire by night. Daytime relies on sword and witchcraft; at night you become stronger and faster but need/crave blood. Skills split into swordsmanship, witchcraft, and vampirism (the strongest).  Combat mixes The Witcher 3’s feel, movement and the use of magic with simpler directional attacks inspired by Kingdom Come. It feels awkward at first but clicks once you get used to it and invest in skills. Flaws include enemies politely taking turns, camera issues, getting stuck on terrain, and especially level scaling, high-level trash mobs become spongy annoyances. Day/night differences are biggest in combat and movement, and some quests are time-of-day locked, which lets you plan smartly.Most choices have consequences and the morality is nicely fuzzy (reminiscent of The Witcher 2). The world and majority of quests are interesting, with standouts like Anca’s questline. Dialogue can feel uneven in tone, and world reactivity is limited, NPCs barely react to blatant vampire powers. There’s an infamy system with Brencis’ court, but not much beyond direct quest consequences. The near-total lack of stealth also feels like a missed opportunity for a night stalker creature you are. Music, sound, and English voice acting are strong and very Witcher-like. 

Visually it’s pretty but uneven (good models, mixed animations and textures). Performance is the usual UE5 story: not unplayable, but I had a post-prologue crash and VRAM spikes with particles on Linux/Proton. Patches have helped, but UE5 is still UE5. 

In summary, I expected a mediocre Witcher 3 clone and found something better: an imperfect game made with real experience, an engaging world, and the courage to use bold limiting mechanics. That ambition deserves respect.  I really enjoyed The Blood of Dawnwalker. It’s a good game, and even better foundations for a potentially great saga.

TLDR: Expect more of Shadow of Mordor, Far Cry and Mass Effect 3* than Witcher, Gothic, VtM Bloodlines. Needless to say, RP here is more about skill trees and narrative 'TV channels' than character roleplay or skill/perk checks in dialogue. Though very uneager, I do think it qualifies to be called a 'western' RPG. It's still a very good game with moments of meaningful agency.

First the technical part - this game is yet another unfortunate victim of Unreal Engine 5, which includes stuttering and eye watering blur. While optimization could be better, I felt like I had more or less smooth experience, excluding one-two areas such as densely populated city. Regarding TAA, I am happy to say that it can be disabled with an edit of .ini file and the game actually looks good without grainy/artefact look - which is rare, because in some games TAA is either impossible to disable completely (Avowed) or makes the game too terrible looking (Cyberpunk 2077), so if you prefer sharpness of image over blurry softened edges - this game thankfully can provide.

Now the gameplay - the opening sequence may create a false impression that the architecture of the game follows other western RPGs with settlements densely-filled with npcs, dialogue and quests with varying options and lasting consequences. The feeling you get when the prologue is over and you just enter the open world is intoxicating and I want to give a great praise just for that - always nice to disenchant my game impotence. 

Sadly, many players may soon feel burnt and think that the game offers nothing more than ubi-style outpost clearing with 1-2 quests per settlement and 'swiping' the map clean of points of interest a-la witcher 3 question marks. That is mostly the case, although playing for a while longer you realize there is more than meets the eye - the quests are there, dialogue is there and choices do matter - it's just that they are eclipsed with majority of content you will do. The core gameplay loop is 1) bit of dialogue 2) traveling/scanning with 'witcher sense' 3) combat  4) OPTIONAL: trivial choice at the end like spare someones life or engage with moral dilemma, such as clear the bandit outpost only to have their boss beg for mercy in exchange for trinket or knowledge. You still ultimately clear the outpost.

People that complain about 'janky combat' amuse me. You don't know jank until you played original two Gothics. Combat is not janky, maybe the animations are a bit. Once you understand the controls, it becomes enjoyable and you have full control over its flow. Yes, some things are counter intuitive - for example, if you are cornered (literally), witcher 3 players may think pressing space with a direction will allow you to dash through enemy ranks and change position; here it won't work and you just dash towards enemies and get kicked in the face. To achieve what you want, you actually press [E] during combat and you teleport behind enemy back. Yes, the movement in combat is not just barrel-roll dodge that nullifies all damage and crit-attack from back. And that's refreshingly good. Still, you better enjoy this combat system, since you will be doing it entirety of the game - there is no stealth-as-substitute to combat and little to none pacifist speechcraft.

I enjoyed very much the time system in this game and feel like players will like  the game more if they come to terms with it instead of running for nexusmods. Yes, it's a questionable thing like saving with Schnapps in Kingdom Come, but it's purpose is clear - makes the urgency real, instead of 'save Ciri ASAP, but not before winning all Gwent tournaments'. This also finally creates something RPGs miss - because you are time constrained, you cannot help and save everyone, meaning that picking callous/indifferent/neutral options in dialogue/quests actually make sense  not just RP or narrative wise, but also mechanically. In normal cases, you just 100% clear the game to get most XP, ignoring that the protagonist would unlikely go on every errand such as clear rats from basement or deliver fish barrel across entire map. Saying 'no' to people, being neutral or even leaving persons in danger to their fate actually felt impactful.

I don't want to police people into 'correct playstyle' since everyone ultimately plays however they want, especially singleplayer games. I have a friend who plays Hitman by giving himself god mode and infinite ammo and he just runs around with fire axe murdering entirety of the level. However, I must urge you (if interested in this game) NOT to go online looking for guides, NOT to reload save when you get an outcome in dialogue/quest you dislike and NOT to use walkthrough. Trust me, even when you feel strong inclination such as 'find X item f*ck knows where', the gameplay becomes much more interesting when you embrace time-constrained ambiguity. Yes, you will not be able to get 100% 'synchronisation' in a single playthrough. This just makes the choices in first playthrough and subsequent playthroughs more meaningful. Sadly, majority of gamers will just ignore this and just save scum and use guides even in their first playthroughs...

Narrative-wise I have no complaints besides some direction and (story) pacing. The premise of the game and opening is so powerful, it can carry you throughout the game with infrequent reinforcement mid and late game. This game has a rare success of answering the question 'why should *I* give a f*ck?', explaining why would protagonist go through all this instead of taking it as given because *you*, the player, bought the game and will play it anyway - a good litmus test is that the player motivation works even if the protagonist is imagined incredibly cynical, selfish and borderline nihilist. However, sometimes game becomes awkward when you are supposed to feel sad about npc you saw once and already forgot the name or feel romantic connection to a person whose 'chemistry' is comparable to Dexter Morgan, although this may be intentional representation of autistic women (and protagonist) in videogames. I doubt it's the case, as the game sometimes even explicitly says 'man I struggle at this, anyway here is exposition, followed by a invisible variable going +1 to mark bonding'.

Endings and ultimate conclusion left a both positive and negative aftertaste. Positive, because I greatly appreciate the 'Slide-show' style ending that tells us about impact of our choices and fates of people we met. Negative, because I disliked the post-credits scene. Developers, people who play videogames about medieval Europe, vampires, witchcraft and swordplay do not want to see *that*. Ending identical to a film 'Dracula Untold'. I just hope they declare it non-canon. But hey, I am open to be proved wrong and they give us a proper VtM Bloodlines successor.

I feel like this is a quintessential example of 'Very Good, but not a Masterpiece', in russian terms - Zaebis, but not Ohuet. With time, it will likely earn the status of Mad Max or Sleeping Dogs with youtubers making video essays 'Dawnwalker is underrated gem'. It's content is highly eclectic, which combines both good and bad parts of various games, including those I've mentioned in TLDR section. 

*On ME3 - think endless corridors with hordes of repeating 5-6 enemy types minus the companions. Narrative setup, movement through a combat arena, further movement, another wave, another arena, and eventually a scripted climax. Sometimes I felt - Jesus, game, I think it's enough, no need to go through more waves of monsters in this quest...

This negative review is probably telling more about myself than about the game.

I'm not gonna talk about the performance issues, nor the occasional jank in movements, combats, NPCs behavior. Those aspects can be improved, and might with future patches, and they are extensively talked about in other reviews.

The graphics are good enough, if not a bit weird at times, especially concerning characters. The story is really nice, the overall ambiance is very good and the music is amazing. By all accounts, this should be a positive review. 

But my gripe with the game is apparently what other people love: The whole design mechanic around the time management. I know this simply means this game is not made for people like me, but I'd still like to talk about it.

To put it simply, this game makes me feel bad about how I play it. The FOMO is overwhelming. I'm obviously okay with the principle of exclusive quests and decisions: If I do this, I'm locked out of that. No problem, I was aware of this before buying. I was just not aware of how far this was pushed. Engaging with what I find by roaming will lock me out of content. Getting curious will lock me out of content. Leveling up will lock me out of content. I ended up paralyzed by my own indecisiveness. I ignored so much stuff that crossed my path. What is usually driven by curiosity was instead met with apathy. "Ho, a trail of blood, corpses to investigate... Why would I do that? Why would I engage with this content? The game made the sense of urgency clear, both narratively and mechanically. I have no reason whatsoever to engage with that, this has nothing to do with my objective."

Eventually, I got to a city...And the feeling got even worse. Instead of wanting to look around, enjoy the area, I just had to go to my objective. I have no time to stop. The game made it clear. I shouldn't stop. Look around? Sure. But don't engage with anything. Here's the problem: maybe I did have time to stop and engage with all of this. Maybe I didn't. There is no way to know without already knowing what the rest of the game will demand from me. So instead of making choices based on curiosity or role-playing, I make them based on uncertainty. The game keeps asking me, in effect, “are you sure this is worth your time?” And eventually, my answer becomes “probably not".

Concerning the leveling up part, I eventually got to a point where I have 13 skills points unused, because spending them would pass time. I fully believe this game is balanced around that cost, but that doesn't change how it feels: leveling up is robbing me of playtime, prompting me to stay underleveled just so I can have more of the game.

I just don't believe in making the player second guess themselves for every single thing.

It's an RPG telling me that if I engage with the RPG, I get less RPG. What could have been done with branching quests, conflicting objectives, and narrative consequences, was instead done with a "FOMO bar" on the top-right. Sure, the result is the same, but how I experience it as a player is vastly different.

Now, you could of course see what you missed by restarting the game all over again, but...

Will you?

When it was first announced that The Blood of Dawnwalker was being developed by veterans from The Witcher 3 team under Bandai Namco, I was incredibly excited yet "skeptical" about the chosen genre an openworld dark fantasy Action-RPG. It is a rather generic blend of genres that requires plenty of surprising elements to truly become a "Grande" masterpiece. 

The setting 14th century Europe, ravaged by plague and brutal warfare is fascinating. The medieval European scenery, forest landscapes, and detailed urban environments feel incredibly dense and immersive. The day-night gameplay variation is striking combat styles and exploration differ so much between day and night that it feels like playing two distinct characters. By day, Coen operates as a human, utilizing a sword, elemental magic, and investigative skills reminiscent of a Witcher. By night, he unleashes his vampire form, gaining access to supernatural abilities, brutal executions, and parkour-style rooftop navigation. 

Open-world exploration is free from time constraints, but undertaking main or critical missions causes time to advance. This means you cannot complete every single mission in a single playthrough. The Witcher 3 DNA is palpable the dialogue writing, dark atmosphere, and morally grey consequences are executed masterfully. The time-progression system adds significant replayability, as quest choices genuinely impact the storyline. 

However, the parry and combat systems feel a bit stiff. The swordplay attempts a directional parry approach (similar to Kingdom Come) but can feel clunky at times, and the camera lock-on lacks precision. Personally, I also found some side quests and minor open-world activities to be somewhat monotonous.

Updated review on a 4090M laptop and a Z1E Rog Ally X.

FIRST the devs need to properly configure how this game syncs save files on steam as graphics configuration is mixed with save file so when you are playing across different PC specs; you have to readjust settings each time! So going from a DLSS PC to a AMD GPU PC; you have to reselect all graphic settings each time. This is something Steamworks documentation explictly tells devs NOT to do and even indie game devs can get this right but apparently not Witcher 3 veteran devs. This is a joke.

Overall recommendation based on state of performance and in-game optimisation is watch and wait. Unless you have a beefy PC or willing to put up with performance level upscaling and frame gen ON.

Gameplay and Mechanics

On keyboard and mouse the controls are somewhat awkward and often hectic in fights. Examples of this include; in inventory you have to click on an item and then press ENTER to equip/unequip. You can't just hover over and click like most games. In traversal you have the ability E to shadow phase/step but on keyboard it feels slightly awkward to use as you can hold e and select a spot to phase to (with a range limitation like a turn based mechanic almost) or press e repeatdly to essentially continue to stutter phase in real-time. 

The in-game combat and UI is very similiar to Kingdom Come 2 (so if you like it there then you will adjust much faster here). The looting, menu UI, in-game interactions, NPC, world setting etc. is essentially Witcher 3 with Dawnwalker mod (this is not a criticism rather just reflection of Witcher origin of the devs). One thing is combat can get hectic very fast even if just fighting 2 NPCs and it gets hard to respond when both are simultaneously attacking you. On story/fair difficulties etc. (which is standard or easy) you can have incoming block and attack animations showing where enemy is attacking from and block/dodge accordingly (let KC2). However, even changing difficulty to fair was at times difficult to react to multiple incoming attack direction queues so the only viable strategy if dealing with mobs is either try draw 1 NPC away (not always practical nor does in-game A.I allow that level of fidelity gameplay) or spam dodge (which depletes stamina quick without perfect dodge). 

Speaking of perfect dodge; there is no time slow down, no real reward or momentary i-frame type of mechanic from perfect dodge. The only reward is you consume no stamina whereas perfect blocking unlocks a momentary window for attack. If you compare to something like Stellarblade; the issue here both perfect dodge and block requires similiar level of skill/user interaction/reaction needed (yes you can perfect dodge in more directions vs. only perfect block in a single direction). But when you are fighting a mob (which is almost always), blocking let alone perfect blocking becomes increasingly difficult not because skill issue rather attacks are coming at you at same time so you have a choice to either block one get hit by another or only viable way for nil damage is to dodge. You can see where I'm going with this which is essentially in-game design choices/mechancis encourage players to block over dodge but blocking vs. 2 or more NPCs in a fight is significantly less viable than dodging. When you add perfect dodge mechanic with minimal reward (and dodge obviously takes you away from chance at counter striking as you increase distance between you and targets); you feel as a player unfairly pushed towards a certain play style that doesn't cohesively present as a holistic package in mob fights. That is; if you want to reduce damage taken then you can only dodge against mobs which in turn takes you away from counter strike opportunity so you have to reposition to strike only to have enemy NPCs ready for another attack animation coming at you same time from multiple directions so blocking becomes not viable and this gameplay loop repeats.

Performance on 4090M

There is noticeable stuttering in open world for me likely from first playthrough shader compiling but will update as I go. I would also recommend playing with a controller over KB+M as I found KB+M to be clunky at times including when interacting in inventory or when fighting as you have to do directional attacks (WASD + LMB), directional blocks/dodge (WASD + RMB/LCTRL) then use keys like Q/S/1,2,3,4 etc for abilities and quick items. This combo in Dawnwalker's fast paced combat even at fair difficulty can become hectic. I found actions like crouching (LCTRL) felt laggy as in you press LCTRL and there's a noticeable delay on magnitude of almost a second or so.

This game runs sub-optimal at start and in starting village area with frequent UE5 traversal stutters even after multiple playthroughs and reloads. On 4090M/13900HX it runs about 40FPS at DLAA Ultra with no FG (60~90FPS with DLSS FG with AVG ~75FPS). The issue seems to be shader compilation with initial playthrough experiencing classic issues like interrupted frame pacing with new shaders loading with new animations or new cutscenes. Example is intro video once you start a game which I believe all cinematic is capped at 30FPS but the entire cinematic intro played out with micro and noticeable longer stutters from fame pacing where average frametime is ~33.3ms but I saw spikes >55ms every 15 seconds or so to give you an idea. It was definitely noticeable enough and frequent enough to distract away from otherwise good cinematic background story. 30FPS cap on cutscenes in general can lead to more stuttering experience for viewers.

Performance on Rog Ally X Z1E (30W Turbo)

The game is barely playable on Z1E. On FSR Performance everything set to LOW with FSR FG ON; I get 45~60FPS with majority sitting around 50FPS gameplay and just roaming no combat. This is with FSR FG ON so without you are looking at sub 30FPS which is atrocious. So this game will not be playable on anything but Z2E or the new Intel G3 Arc Extreme handhelds. Good luck to the steam deck zealots that will try to run and defend this game is playable using multiple proton hacks including LSFG and FSR 4 mod lol.

Summary

I would actually recommend watch and wait for this game to get more performance patches and optimisations especially if you're on lower end hardware. The game is definitely playable on something like a 4060/4070 PC but expect 1080P with upscaling and FG to hit more than 60FPS.

Whenever a game markets itself by highlighting the involvement of developers who previously worked on beloved titles, I tend to get a little worried about the outcome. We've seen plenty of projects rely heavily on the reputation of their creators, only to fall short of expectations.

Thankfully, The Blood of Dawnwalker is a wonderful exception to that pattern.

Not only does it avoid becoming another disappointment, but it also lays an incredibly promising foundation for what could become a fantastic RPG franchise for years to come.

For the debut title of a studio founded by the former director of The Witcher 3, Rebel Wolves has done an impressive job.

The story is engaging from beginning to end, supported by excellent RPG mechanics, a wonderful dialogue system, and a dynamic world that genuinely reacts to your decisions and actions. The sense that your choices matter adds a great deal to the overall experience and makes the journey feel much more personal.

The combat is enjoyable, and the music and voice acting are fantastic, further elevating the atmosphere and bringing the world and its characters to life.

Of course, the game isn't without its shortcomings.

There are a few bugs and optimization issues that occasionally get in the way. While the combat is satisfying at first, its relative simplicity becomes more noticeable over time, and I wish there were more variety in the boss encounters.

The visuals are also somewhat inconsistent. Although the game has its moments, the overall graphical quality could use some improvement, particularly when it comes to facial animations, which sometimes fail to do justice to the performances behind them.

These issues prevent the game from reaching even greater heights, but they never overshadow what Rebel Wolves has accomplished here.

For me, The Blood of Dawnwalker is an 8.5/10.

It's a fantastic journey and an incredibly strong debut for a new studio. More importantly, it feels like the beginning of something much bigger.

If this is what Rebel Wolves can deliver with its first game, I genuinely can't wait to see where they take this world next.

Although the game has been very good overall, it fails miserably in two aspects of the combat system:

1 - The environment becomes a major barrier. You simply get stuck on any prop in the environment during battles, preventing fluid movement—especially when dodging or walking. It feels like the player's hitbox becomes massive and easily collides with anything, preventing you from passing through paths that visibly have plenty of space to get through, yet the character simply seems to be held back by an invisible wall.

2 - When entering battles, you are trapped in an arena formed by invisible walls that forces the player to face the enemy; this is the most ridiculous and absurd part of all.

3 - The camera position, with the character out of alignment from its center, causes a huge annoyance when dealing with battles and a combat system that naturally requires the player to have a more centralized view to help perceive what is happening around them with better precision.

4 - The combat system itself is good, but there is one detail that completely ruins the balance: the enemies do not stagger or react to hits. For example, when the player hits an enemy, the enemy counterattacks almost instantly, giving the feeling that the player's attacks are very irrelevant, as if the enemy doesn't feel pain or anything. This completely breaks the immersion and is a completely unnecessary type of pressure, since the system itself and the NPC combat AI are very good. They keep the pressure up, so the player needs a way to relieve that pressure.

Suggestions for Improvement

Fix what is considered a bug, such as the character's movement being blocked by the environment during battles.

Give the player the option to align the camera so that the character is centered on the screen.

Allow the player to flee from battles. Definitely never create invisible barriers to confine the player when a battle starts, especially in an open world—it is simply disgusting.

Make the player's attacks have a more significant impact on NPCs.

What Should Not Be Changed

The combat system itself and the NPC aggressiveness should not be touched; those are excellent. Let me say it again: what actually needs to be changed or added is making the NPC feel the hit landed by the player more.

[h2]The Blood of Dawnwalker: Thirty Days in Vale Sangora[/h2]

The Blood of Dawnwalker has quite a few things that clearly need improvement, and I still really liked it. Its flaws are obvious, but the things it does well mattered much more to me by the end.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3809972421

☾ [b]Story & Setting[/b]

The game takes place in 14th-century Europe, in the fictional region of Vale Sangora, devastated by war, disease and the Black Death. With humanity weakened, vampires (here and after - [i]vrakhiri[/i]) stop hiding and begin openly taking control under knyaz Brencis. You play as Coen, a young man who becomes a Dawnwalker - human during the day and vrakhiri during the night. His family ends up at the center of the conflict, and you are given thirty days and thirty nights to save them.

Personally, I really enjoyed the plot. Eastern European dark fantasy with vampires, plague, superstition and old folklore was always going to win me over.

Vale Sangora feels appropriately miserable. Villages are dirty, people are frightened and superstitious, religion and vrakhiri politics hang over everything. The music, locations, lighting and overall art direction are absolutely gorgeous - this game is ridiculously beautiful to look at.

I also ended up liking Coen much more than I expected. He feels like an actual protagonist while still leaving room to shape him through your choices. By the end I was genuinely attached to him.

☾ [b]Day & Night[/b]

During the day Coen is human, while at night he becomes a vrakhiri. By day you fight with a sword and develop Witchcraft abilities; by night you gain vampiric abilities, feeding and supernatural mobility. Equipment differs too, so the transformation is more than cosmetic.

I liked this system a lot. Both sides still rely heavily on the same combat foundation, especially parrying, but switching between them gives the game some much-needed variety.

At night, Coen’s hunger can get dangerous enough that he may feed on almost anyone - even important story characters - which is a genuinely great idea. The problem is that keeping him fed is so easy that this almost never becomes a real threat. Dawnwalker comes up with a wonderfully cruel system and then seems too afraid to actually make the player suffer for ignoring it.

☾ [b]Combat[/b]

The system is directional. On keyboard, movement inputs determine the direction of your attacks, while incoming attacks show where the enemy is about to strike from. You can block, dodge or parry, then mix those actions with human, Witchcraft or vampiric abilities.

The first half was genuinely fun, and eventually the timing became natural and combat started feeling strangely relaxing. Unfortunately, once you properly learn how to parry, the difficulty drops [i]hard[/i].

I played on High difficulty and, outside of one boss fight against Bakir, I never felt seriously threatened. Even skull-marked enemies were manageable if I kept parrying correctly. After around fifty hours, the repetition became much more noticeable.

☾ [b]Alchemy & Enemy Variety[/b]

The game has a large crafting system with healing items, stamina consumables, weapon applications and plenty of other things you can make. The strange part is that I barely needed any of it. I mostly crafted healing items because once I was comfortable with parrying and abilities, most enemies could be handled without preparation.

That feels like wasted potential. I would have loved enemies with specific resistances or weaknesses that forced me to prepare accordingly.

The world has interesting supernatural lore, with Sanzhani, uriashi, kobolds and other folkloric beings. Unfortunately, the combat bestiary doesn’t live up to that worldbuilding. You fight undead, spirits, wolves, boars, bears, kobolds and a small number of other recurring enemies. For a fantasy world drawing on this much folklore, I really wanted more variety.

☾ [b]Romance[/b]

There are three possible romance paths - Marat, Lacra and Anca - and I developed Coen’s relationships with both Lacra and Anca. I liked how gradual they felt: there is time to actually talk, get to know them and watch the dynamic change. Out of the two, Anca was definitely my favorite.

My problem is the payoff. Both romances left me with roughly the same feeling: Coen gets close to someone, the relationship becomes intimate, and then the whole thing basically ends there. The poor man gets used for sex and sent back into being even lonelier than he already was.

The buildup is good, which makes the abruptness more frustrating. Coen has had a rough enough month already. Let the poor bastard keep a girlfriend.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3798307388

☾ [b]The 30-Day Limit[/b]

You have thirty days and thirty nights to complete Coen’s main objective, but time does not constantly pass while you explore. Instead, days and nights are divided into segments, and quests, training and certain actions consume them. At first, I loved this idea. I wanted the game to put me under pressure, make me sacrifice things and force me to choose what mattered most. In practice, it was much more forgiving than I expected.

I completed essentially every piece of story content I cared about and developed Coen pretty much however I wanted. When I was about to finish, I still had roughly seven days left, with mostly minor stuff remaining: kill a creature, rescue someone random, find some treasure. I wish it were way stricter. If the entire premise is built around limited time, I want the game to make me feel that limitation. Instead, I did everything that mattered to me and still had an entire in-game week left for random monster hunting.

☾ [b]Infamy & Choices[/b]

One system that worked extremely well for me was Infamy. As Coen becomes more notorious, Brencis takes increasingly aggressive measures against him. Guards start recognizing you, the world becomes more hostile and ordinary NPCs react differently. Eventually, openly walking through Svartrau becomes genuinely inconvenient because guards recognize you almost everywhere.

I also enjoyed the flexibility in the ending. Different allies can influence your route, you can make a deal with Brencis, take less heroic approaches or even leave the valley. There is also a particularly interesting outcome tied to an optional quest that can be missed entirely, which I found almost by accident.

☾ [b]Overall[/b]

Despite everything I have complained about, I came away from The Blood of Dawnwalker feeling very positive about it. I liked Coen, Vale Sangora, the characters, the folklore and the general atmosphere. I enjoyed playing someone who exists somewhere between human and vampire, and when the credits rolled, I wanted another game.

I want Rebel Wolves to keep developing this world, learn from what didn’t work here, expand the bestiary, make alchemy useful, make higher difficulties more demanding and give Coen’s relationships more emotional payoff.

And if you are going to give me thirty days to save my family again, please make me actually afraid of wasting them next time.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is not a perfect RPG, and I don’t think its current price reflects how rough some of its systems still are. But the foundation is strong, the world has personality, and I genuinely want to see what Rebel Wolves could do with a second attempt.

[b]For all its flaws, this is a world I would happily come back to.[/b]

First, it's the combat. The auto-targeting is abysmal. Other games target in the exact same way that feel so much better than this, so there's no excuse for it to be so bad. Fighting multiple enemies at once feels horrid because the auto targeting will flicker to things you aren't aiming at, particularly things that are behind what you actually want to hit.

And then there's the block / dodge system. As a concept, fine. Other games do it, it works. Here's where this game fucks up:

- If you are holding block, you can not dodge. This is basic functionality. While you are holding block, if you press to dodge in a direction, the dodge should cancel your blocking stance and make you dodge. This is a no brainer and it's wild that it made it to release this way.

- Stamina exists to limit two things; turtling, and spamming attacks. It serves this purpose well, which again, other games do this. In this game, attacks have virtually zero hit stun. This completely kills offensive momentum. When you attack an enemy and land a hit, they should be briefly stunned/staggered so you can follow up with another hit. The thing that is meant to limit combo chains is either running out of stamina (which then endangers your defense), or being attacked by another enemy from the flank while your guard is down. Some boss enemies have mechanics to also power through spam attacks, unique to each boss.

When attacks have no stagger, it makes offense completely suck. After you get in 2-3 attacks, the enemy will just super armor through any hit stun and attack you. Between this and the janky targeting and camera controls in combat, the only viable strategy in combat is to try to perfect dodge and block everything, attack ~2 times, then repeat. Over and over. This is boring, this doesn't feel fun, this isn't well designed. It especially feels bad in combat against multiple enemies, and it especially feels bad with the janky targeting system.

Other mechanical flaws:

- The movement is generally janky. It feels clumsy and unresponsive. It's not horrendous, but it needs work.

- You can not crouch with a weapon drawn. You can not cancel your run into a crouch, either. This is just one of many things that makes movement feel clunky, but at least one I can identify the exact cause of. This game suffers from a lot of coding clumsiness where if you are inputting one command (run) you can not cancel it with another command (crouch). This is the same thing that afflicts the inability to cancel blocking into dodges.

- You can press to hold walk (terrible, goofy animation especially when turning), but can't press to hold sprint. Sprinting is toggle only. Why? Every other game has this setting. Let me choose, please.

- You shouldn't take fall damage at night. I can teleport everywhere, but if I fall 30 feet, I die. That's very silly. At night, my character should automatically teleport to the ground before impact.

- You should be able to drink blood from things that you kill after they are dead. I can maybe understand what they were trying to do here, that they wanted your health to be lowered after combat and not so easy to sustain, but it's just not working and it doesn't make sense. The alternative is running around drinking from deer's, rabbits and rats after combat. That's not fun or satisfying for the vampire fantasy when a fresh corpse is right in front of me to drink from. Having to run around hunting animals just to heal up feels really lame, and like a chore.

I definitely recommend The Blood of Dawnwalker. I’m still relatively early in the game, so these are more my impressions so far than a final review, but I’m genuinely enjoying it.

The story has captured my attention, and I really like the world, its lore, and the characters I've encountered so far. The game feels narrative-quest-driven, which works well for me, and I’m curious to see where the story goes.

One of my biggest surprises has actually been the combat. I’m usually not someone who gets particularly invested in learning complex combat mechanics. In many games, I'm perfectly happy with a relatively simple “hit things until they die” approach. :) But here, the directional sword-fighting system actually managed to engage me. I found myself wanting to understand it and use it properly, which is pretty unusual for me.

I also really appreciate how the developers handled accessibility here. If you don't enjoy the directional blocking system, you can essentially opt out of it and accept a higher stamina cost instead. I think that's a great compromise: the mechanic is there for people who enjoy it, without forcing everyone to engage with it.

I also like the difference between Coen during the day and at night. Having different abilities depending on his state adds another layer to character progression and makes you think about where you spend your points and how you use your time.

And time really is a currency in this game.

For the most part, I think the time system is fair. You understand quite early that you won't necessarily be able to do everything, and your decisions about where to go and which quests to pursue have consequences. As someone who is very much an open-world completionist and a bit of a hoarder, this is naturally painful for me — I WANT TO DO EVERYTHING. But I can accept it as part of the game's design.

What I particularly don't like is spending that same limited time simply to progress or unlock skills. That feels unnecessarily restrictive to me. I can understand limiting how much the player can accomplish through quests and choices — that's meaningful. But losing part of such an important resource just because I progressed my character feels different. Perhaps it's intended to prevent the player from becoming too powerful too quickly, but at least at this point in the game, I think it's excessive.

As for exploration, I wouldn't say the open world itself is overflowing with things to discover. A lot of my exploration so far has revolved around quests and marked points of interest rather than simply wandering around and constantly discovering unexpected things. But since this is clearly a narrative-driven RPG, I don't consider that a major problem.

Overall, though, I'm having a lot of fun. I like the characters, I find the story compelling, I enjoy the lore, and — surprisingly for me — I genuinely enjoy the combat system. The game has managed to make me care about mechanics that I usually don't pay much attention to, and I think that's quite an achievement.

Definitely recommended based on my experience so far. I'll be curious to see whether my opinion about the time system changes as I get further into the game.

Well, while playing this game I often found myself asking, “Am I actually enjoying this? Is this fun?” Not a great sign, and despite me being a fan of vampire games and the Witcher, I ultimately have to land on a thumbs down for this game because the answer was often no. 

The combat was fun initially, but once I mastered it became really stale. Best game I've played in years. Definitely a must play if you're a fan of Witcher 3, Blade, or any vampire media at all.

Now, it isn't without blemishes, but for a studio's first title I'd say it's really impressive. The vision the company has for this game is also very bold, as it has already announced plans to take the Dawnwalker title to the present day. 

And it isn't bold without a reason, there are real glimpses of something special here. Vampires are every bit the terrifying creatures that haunt the night that Twilight successfully erased for a while. They're strong, arrogant, and prone to a particular eldritch corruption from another realm that all but ensures insanity and a twisted visage with age. The lore, although obfuscated to a fault here, seems to be pointing at a greater narrative.

Now, I did say there were blemishes, and there are. First is just how little lore is fed to you throughout the game. It seems that the game believes that players are only looking forward to perk points -- or skill manuals -- or gold, when what I really wanted was a mission where I got to read some information about Dawnwalkers and Anachora (the eldritch realm that is the source of vampiric corruption), which I only got tiny bits of. 
I'm very used to obfuscation in a narrative in order to keep the player invested in the mysteries, but I did at points get the impression that it was less hiding lore -- and more that I had questions which the devs hadn't thought of yet, and thus there were no answers.

Another thing is that the villains are quite imposing, but lack depth. Everyone likes a monstrous vampire, and that's about what you get here. There is not much mention of overarching structures (like vampire clans), just a clique that took over Vale Sangora when the opportunity presented itself. So you're left with these ancient vampires that feel more like petty warlords, and to be fair, that is the intention with Bakir, but felt lacking otherwise to the other vampires.

Immersion is also something that is quite weak here. Sometimes people will straight up not mention on the fact you're a vampire: common soldiers will not flee under any circumstances, people you've helped will not mention that you're (clearly) a vampire, and those who do, often do not react as terrified as they should.

People -- and there's no getting around this -- do not really react like medieval serfs would. Almost all of the people in this game act like modern people. Some of the Manumits pretty much act like petty nobles if they had modern sensibilities. It's weird, and if you're expecting the level of immersion that KCD2 offers, it really won't be found here.

Some gameplay choices are also quite baffling. The weight system is entirely unnecessary and you'll eventually have so much crafting material will occupy 90% of your space, so you'll just have to shove a bunch of them into the storage that the fast travel shrines have. This is to the game's detriment.

A design choice, and my personal pet peeve, is that the enemies scale with you. I'm (mostly) fine with scaling for bosses, but the normal enemies will scale despite the fact that the gameplay loop has you go through increasingly harder territories (from Ambrus' into Bakir's into Xanthe's). Let the easier areas be outscaled! The player earned it!

Perhaps the most polarizing choice was setting a maximum time for this game -- 30 days. Now, it is both a choice for immersion (the villain won't just stand around waiting), as well as intrinsic to the game's day and night cycle, where you're a vampire at night and warlock/human at day.
It is.. an interesting system. And I can imagine very tempting for devs involved with Witcher 3, famously a game so large that many did not ever get to finish it. I understand what they were going for, but personally, I'm a "do everything before the final mission" type of guy, and so I was displeased with the system.

Another issue is that time limit also constrains how many perks you can realistically achieve and invest in a playthrough, and traversal/mobility is locked behind the perk tree. These perks increase only your traversal speed and don't affect combat, and therefore are not worth a perk because they're only QoL. This only serves to make your experience worse, and they should be unlocked automatically by reaching certain level milestones.

TL;DR: Despite it all, it's a great game that I enjoyed thoroughly. I remain optimistic that all the issues here pointed can be fixed by a sequel or even DLC as, at its core, this is an incredibly promising project.

I can see why many draw parallels between The Blood of Dawnwalker and The Witcher series. Whilst the game shares many similarities, such as the overall style and the music having a noticeable resemblance to The Witcher, I would happily say that this game can stand on its own. It does enough differently that I never really felt like I was simply playing The Witcher again, which is probably for the best considering we already have The Witcher.

I’ve really enjoyed playing it so far, and I’ve completed one of the game’s endings. I do admit I rather rushed it to get to the ending... but I tend to do that on my first playthrough for some reason. [i]No idea why... mysterious.[/i] I do plan to play it again, though, and explore other side quests, tasks, and the other endings. This will presumably involve me actually taking my time this time, although I have made similar claims before.

I do want to say, though, that from the “major” side quests, there does seem to be less content than, say, The Witcher 3 had. That’s just my opinion, though, and I’m not blaming the game for it. I think the amount of content I got was worth it, for me at least. Considering I rushed through some of it, I probably shouldn’t complain too much.

Now for some nitpicks. I found it rather weird that the vampire form has no night vision, considering that Coen’s eyes do glow, signalling that he could see? You would think this would be one of the more obvious benefits of becoming a vampire, unless the glowing eyes are purely decorative, in which case they are doing an excellent job of looking like they have a purpose.

I hear people give the combat criticism, but I personally also enjoyed it. I can see it not suiting everyone. Overall, I had no real issue with it. Perhaps I’m simply at the stage of my life where I have accepted that combat in a game is occasionally going to involve me waving a weapon around whilst wondering what exactly my character is doing.

In any case, I found the way they handled the 30-day time system interesting, in a good way. I had some reservations when I first heard about it, as having a limited amount of time in an open-world RPG sounded rather restrictive. But it ended up working better than I expected, so I can't really complain about it.

I did notice towards the end of the game that the amount of time left didn’t matter as much, but in general I think it is a unique system. One thing I found weird was that you also use up time when levelling up your skills, which does make you wonder what exactly Coen is doing whilst standing in a menu deciding which skill he would like to learn. Presumably staring into the middle distance and contemplating life. That said, I can see why it works from a replayability perspective, since you can change up your build on another playthrough.

Performance was generally fine for me on the ultra preset, with only occasional dips when there was a lot happening on screen.

Anyhow, I really enjoyed this game. I haven’t gone into every aspect of it since I'm not an actual game critic, but I do want to mention that I found the quests good. I’ll definitely be playing it again, which is probably the most convincing endorsement I can give it, considering I have apparently already forgotten to take things slowly and carefully explore everything.

[b] The Blood of Dawnwalker [/b] is one of the best action RPGs I've played in recent years. From the very beginning, you can feel that the people behind the game have experience working on The Witcher 3. It's not a copy of that game, but a similar way of telling the story, building the atmosphere, and writing the characters is very noticeable.

The story and its main ideas are really well written. It quickly manages to get you interested, and the world full of vampires, magic, and medieval conflicts leaves plenty of room for interesting stories. At many points, I felt like I was playing something that could've been another dark RPG from the creators of The Witcher 3. For a fan of that universe, that's definitely a big plus.

The combat is also very good. For me, it feels a bit like Kingdom Come: Deliverance. It's a bit challenging, but at the same time very satisfying. There's also a good character progression system, with different skills to use, while vampire powers and sorcery let you build your character around your own playstyle. This means you're not locked into one way of playing.

The world itself is unfortunately a bit weaker. Sangorska Valley has the right dark atmosphere, but at times it's just too gloomy and lacking in color. I would've liked to see more life and more variety in the scenery. Instead of a world that really feels alive, we often get something that feels more like a dead and gloomy swamp. The atmosphere is there, but I think the world could've used more variety.

The biggest problem is optimization. And here we unfortunately have the classic Unreal Engine 5 problems. Even on strong hardware, the game can have very poor performance, and Frame Generation, which should help, can also cause problems. Thankfully, the developers are releasing patches regularly, so I hope things will get much better over time.

Despite that, I really like The Blood of Dawnwalker. It's an ambitious RPG with a very good story, great combat, and a lot of freedom when it comes to making decisions. The game is highly replayable, and many situations can be handled in completely different ways each time. You can see that the developers wanted to create something big, and they definitely have a clear idea of what they want to achieve. For me, it's a very solid game that I'd especially recommend to Witcher fans.
