I really love vampires and their folklore. They’ve always been one of my favorite types of stories. What I liked about Dawnwalker is that it actually gives vampires their own identity instead of just recycling the same old formula.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Quests & Time System[/h2]

It really makes you think about which quests are actually worth doing, which abilities you should invest in, and what you’re willing to sacrifice just to save some time. Sometimes that even means leaving innocent people behind, which honestly makes those decisions hit a lot harder.
I think they handled this system really well. It makes your choices feel like they actually matter.
The quests themselves are pretty unique, and some of them have genuinely shocking endings. The way you approach certain quests can change depending on whether it’s day or night, and your decisions can affect other quests later on. I really liked that.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Gameplay[/h2]

The combat is inspired by For Honor, and it’s honestly really fun and addictive. The skill trees are solid and give you different ways to play.
That said, I wasn’t a fan of the Witchcraft tree and mostly ignored it. I also wish there was a stealth system, and the enemy variety could’ve been better.
It’s a shame because the core gameplay is strong. More enemy variety and a stealth option would’ve made it even better.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Story[/h2]

Coen is just a young peasant trying to save his family from an Elder Vampire and his court, who’ve been controlling Vale Sangora.
The story has some strong moments, but what I enjoyed more was how you have to explore to uncover each character’s past. The game doesn’t just hand you everything through the main story, and finding those details yourself makes the world and characters feel more alive.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]World & Exploration[/h2]

Easily one of the strongest parts of the game. The map isn’t stupidly huge for the sake of being huge, but it never feels empty. Almost every area has something going on, and the longer you spend looking around, the more stuff you end up stumbling into, side quests, items, small rewards, whatever.
What I appreciated is that exploring doesn’t feel like a chore. It actually feels useful, which made me genuinely curious to check places instead of just rushing the main path.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Graphics & Optimization[/h2]

The art direction and graphics look great overall, though there are some areas where the visual quality drops and a few visual glitches show up.
Nothing that ruined the experience for me, but it could’ve been better.
As for the optimization… yeah
Another Unreal Engine 5 game with the same old performance issues.
[hr][/hr]
[h2]Overall[/h2]

I really enjoyed almost every moment of Dawnwalker, and it honestly became my favorite vampire game.
I’m really excited to see where Coen’s journey goes from here. Hopefully, the next game improves some of the issues I mentioned, because Dawnwalker is already a really good start to what could become an amazing saga.

I tried so hard to like this game. I really love open worlds with consequences, grimdark settings and while Vampires are not exactly my favorite sub-culture of fantasy I feel that this game does it incredibly well. The story and worldbuilding are excellent. You feel very early on the call to either do things the efficient way or the ethical way and that carries through for much of the game as I was able to play it. The time system is fine and not as constraining as I initially thought and adds depth to the choices and the order that you make them.

The failings of this game come about in the open world, exploration, combat and stability. There is a popular sentiment among those that play this game that the game is fun but linearly gets less fun the more you play. In particular the gameplay loop is repetitive, the combat is shallow, you have to spend time as a resource to learn your skills, which you have to earn by doing objectives around the map that already take time themselves. Half of your skill tree is only effective during the day and the other half is only effective at night, which means you are wasting one or the other to make your selection more effective. It feels restraining in a way that you cannot play the game you wish to play it.

Combat is a slog and I dread getting caught out by a wolf or a boar on a slightly mountainous terrain where it can potentially outrun me so I can't use my camera to turn around and bail from the fight. I got to about level 45, so it wasn't for lack of trying. Moreover if you fight something on a terrain that has even a slight incline or a fence or a bush Coen will be locked onto an enemy with no hope of being able to hit said enemy because jumping is disabled during combat and you cannot leave "Combat Coen" mode during this time.

Traversal is a pain because the mountains and slight inclines were an afterthought in its design and cannot be effectively climbed. Coen will slide down to an appropriate angle if there is anything greater than a 40 percent incline, even in Vrakhiri form where he can literally walk up straight walls. You can't use your blink (Shadowstep) to go up or down these inclines reliably because you can only go a limited distance unless you have upgraded it.

Most recently I am being forced to drop the game because a specific quest "Shadow in the Woods" ends in an infinite loading screen softlock. I have tried relaunching, loading earlier saves, doing different dialogue options at the end of the quest, turning off Vsync and changing various settings and several other fixes I have read about online to no avail.

Overall I think this game has alot of good concepts and is fun for a time, but it is not the $70 AAA release that it advertises itself as and I could perhaps recommend this game for $20 or $30, but not in its current state.

Long story short: I don't like this game.
To preface this, I have been following the development of this game since it was announced. When it finally released, I waited a few days for the inevitable bug patches before buying it. Once I started playing, however, I was quickly disappointed by a myriad of poor and strange game design choices.

Combat
The combat is not good.
The combination of limited enemy variety (six or seven enemy types) and unchallenging combat means you'll have more or less mastered the system within the first hour. Like many modern "RPGs," the game also suffers from artificial difficulty and time  wasting mechanics.
Enemies are leveled in such a way that you'll frequently have to decide whether you want to fight something the game clearly doesn't want you to fight yet and potentially waste 10+ minutes on a single battle, or simply reload an earlier save and avoid the encounter entirely.
If you're wondering why you'd have to save-scum just to avoid a fight, the answer is simple: the game forces you to fight almost every encounter you stumble across. Want to explore one of the cities and accidentally bump into a guard? Fight. Wander through the woods looking for something and stumble across wolves? Fight. It's tedious and, frankly, strange.
Another unavoidable problem with combat is the map geometry. Every little piece of clutter on the ground is immovable and might as well be an invisible wall. If you're not careful, that random bucket sitting on the ground can literally lead to your death.
Equipment is another system that feels like it exists primarily to waste your time. So far, it seems to add little beyond increasing your damage numbers without providing any meaningful depth.
The weapon arts are similarly uninspired and limited. They do very little damage against enemies around your level and don't add much to the combat.
Before moving on, I also have to give a special shout-out to whoever made the brilliant decision to create multiple armor presets that automatically switch whenever you transition between night and day. Amazing feature. Totally not a pointless time-waster.

The Skill System
Uninteresting and arbitrary.
There is no real explanation for why magic can only be used during the day beyond "that's how the day/night system works." You can experiment with the different skills for a while, figure out which ones you like, and then dump all your skill points into those. There's not much more to it.

The Story
It's not The Witcher. If you're going into this expecting a narrative on that level, curb your expectations. The story struggles to make you care about most of the people involved.
As is often the case with modern RPGs, the villains are probably the most entertaining characters. They aren't particularly deep antagonists, they're fairly one-note—but their respective questlines are at least enjoyable.
Coen is a bland, passive protagonist, which seems to be increasingly standard these days. He rarely has any meaningful opinions about what's happening to or around him.
Most of the side characters are forgettable, and the romances are there, I suppose, if you're looking to check that particular box. Do expect to get invested. Fuck Anca. Don't simp for her.

Worldbuilding
Average at best.
The game tries a lot of interesting ideas, but, in my opinion, none of them are executed particularly well.
Take the Uriashi, for example. Fantasy races seem to be accepted as a normal part of the world, despite this not really being a traditional fantasy setting like The Witcher. Instead, it's an alternate version of our world where history appears to have played out more or less the same way. The game never really explains why the Uriashi still exist.

I'm supposed to believe that multiple Christian groups came to the Valley, encountered an entire population of goat people, and nobody thought to tell the Pope? Nobody called for a crusade? It's a goofy point, and you can obviously ignore it if you want, but the more you think about the setting, the more questions like this start to arise. The vampires, I can understand. They're supernatural creatures. The Uriashi, however, are presumably just normal beings with goat heads.

The Time Mechanic
Most people seem to hate this mechanic for some reason. Personally, I don't think it plays any meaningful role in the game and can basically be ignored.
The passage of time mostly just moves you closer to the inevitable end-credit screen.
If you truly can't 100% the game before the time expires, I would argue that it's intentional. The vast majority of the time you'll spend in the game comes from leveling rather than from organically progressing through the world.

For example, when I first started playing, I took the time system very seriously. Eventually, I got tired of deliberately staying underleveled, so I spent three days leveling up all the random skills I'd unlocked.
This is how a significant portion of your time will be spent, by the way.

Music & Visuals
If you like The Witcher's music, you'll probably like the music here.
Personally, I think the game tries too hard to imitate The Witcher. It draws so many comparisons to it that it never really develops an identity of its own.
The visuals are alright. There are a few locations that look genuinely nice, but those tend to be areas directly tied to story missions, so it's clear they received more attention than the rest of the world.

In Conclusion
I don't like this game. If I could return it, I would.
Maybe someone who enjoys this style of RPG will get more out of it than I did, but for me, the combination of tedious combat, arbitrary systems, bland characters, and a world that constantly reminds me of The Witcher without ever reaching its level made the experience more frustrating than enjoyable.
Thanks for reading my rant. Have a good day.
